summary: The note describes a rise in adult learner enrollment at community colleges since September 1, 2023, as adults seek to start, change, or advance careers. It covers flexible scheduling, employer partnerships, financial aid, lifelong-learning motives, and older learners, with quotes from educators, an employer, and students. It concludes that community colleges are pivotal in providing meaningful, practical adult education.
one_line: Community colleges are seeing rising adult enrollment since fall 2023, offering flexible, workforce-linked, financially supported programs that help adults reskill and keep learning.
key_facts: Since September 1, 2023, community colleges have seen a considerable uptick in enrollment in adult education programs.
Sarah Jacobs, Dean of Adult Education at Lakeside Community College, reports a 40% increase in adult learner enrollment since the fall of 2023.
Lakeside Community College offers programs ranging from IT certification courses to advanced diplomas in Healthcare Management.
Community colleges accommodate working adults with flexible class schedules, online courses, and hybrid learning models.
Angela Ramirez, Director of Workforce Development at Bay City College, says business leaders are regularly invited to dialogue with instructors so the curriculum stays relevant to market needs.
Tom Eastwood, CEO of TechVentures, says graduates of adult education programs are ready to hit the ground running and bring invaluable life experience.
Joshua Dean, a financial aid adviser at Rivertown Community College, reports a considerable increase in funding for adult learners from government sources and private foundations since late 2023.
Financial barriers are addressed through grant programs, tailored payment plans, and scholarships specifically for adult learners.
Alicia Turner of Midtown Community College says many adults enroll in literature or art history classes out of passion, not for career change.
Harold Bing, an Adult Education Counselor at Lakeside, notes a remarkable surge in learners in their 50s and 60s.
Charles Tam, IT program lead at Haven Community College, says his cybersecurity students learn to protect their own businesses and personal lives from digital threats.
Rosa Martinez, a mother of three, enrolled in a nursing program at Lakeside after two decades away from school.
Dave Anderson, a military veteran studying business management, says the program gave him direction and a community of peers who understand the transition.
